title: Magnetic Communication with an Acoustically Actuated Magnetoelectric Resonator and a Quantum Diamond Magnetometer
authors: Christopher T. -K. Lew, Andrew D. M. Charles, Brant C. Gibson, Jean-Philippe Tetienne, David A. Broadway
abstract: Wireless communication via propagating magnetic fields is a communication modality that has recently garnered significant interest for short-to-medium range communication in conductive mediums, such as underwater and underground, where existing approaches utilizing electric fields are highly inefficient. Typical implementations of magnetic communication make use of loop antennas as both the transmitter and receiver, with the sensitivity and frequency response scaling with and inversely with the loop cross-sectional area, respectively. Here, we explore an alternative hybrid magnetic communication system consisting of an highly radiation efficient and compact acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as the transmitter, and a highly sensitive micrometer scale quantum magnetometer based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond as the receiver, with their core properties unconstrained by size. We demonstrate amplitude and phase-encoded transmission and reception of AC magnetic fields at $f_{\mathrm{AC}}$ = 20 kHz, achieving a sensitivity of 50 pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and 1.2 mrad/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, respectively. This work establishes the use of hybrid magnetoelectric resonator and quantum diamond magnetometer communication system as a viable alternative to existing loop-based approaches.
summary: This work presents a novel magnetic communication system pairing an acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as a transmitter with a highly sensitive quantum diamond magnetometer receiver. By demonstrating amplitude and phase-encoded transmission at 20 kHz, the authors establish a viable, compact alternative to traditional loop-based magnetic communication methods for conductive environments.
main_problem: To develop a compact and highly sensitive alternative magnetic communication system for short-to-medium range transmission in conductive media, overcoming limitations of traditional loop antennas.
main_result: The hybrid system combining an acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator transmitter and a quantum diamond magnetometer receiver successfully demonstrated communication, achieving sensitivities of 50 pT/sqrt(Hz) and 1.2 mrad/sqrt(Hz).
method: The system uses amplitude and phase encoding of AC magnetic fields, measured via the spin-echo decay of Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, driven by an acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator.
model_or_system: The platform consists of a transmitter using a multi-layered ME resonator heterostructure and a receiver utilizing a micrometer-scale NV diamond magnetometer. The magnetometry relies on measuring the phase accumulation ($\delta\phi$) via a Hahn-echo sequence.
key_observables: Amplitude and phase sensitivity (50 pT/sqrt(Hz) and 1.2 mrad/sqrt(Hz)), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and magnetic field decay with distance.
important_parameters: Operating frequency ($f_{AC} = 20 	ext{ kHz}$), spin coherence time ($T_2 = 231 \pm 3 \mu	ext{s}$), and field decay proportional to $1/d^3$ in the near-field.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is residual laser-intensity noise, although the theoretical shot-noise limit is calculated to be $0.33 	ext{ pT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the hybrid system, the AC magnetometry measurement using Hahn-echo sequences, the successful transmission/reception using OOK and BPSK modulation, and the decay of the magnetic field strength with distance in various media.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup, demonstrates communication using modulation schemes (OOK/BPSK), analyzes the magnetic field decay in different media, and provides theoretical appendices on resonator characterization and noise limits.
why_interesting: While the core physics involves quantum sensing (NV centers), the application is in classical communication engineering. However, the use of quantum sensors to measure classical fields at low frequencies makes it relevant to open quantum systems research concerning environmental coupling and noise characterization.
